titre: A Slow Jailer Owed the Prisoner One Hundred Pounds
accroche: In 1679, England closes the loophole by which the Crown imprisoned its subjects outside the kingdom, beyond the reach of the law that protected them at home.
contenu_vulgarise:
Magna Carta of 1215 promises that no free man shall be imprisoned “except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.” It is a principle, not a procedure: it does not say who may invoke it, before whom, or within what time. For more than four centuries, a prisoner who wants to challenge his detention depends on the goodwill of a judge to whom the law leaves complete latitude to hear a petition for habeas corpus, or let it sleep.

The Crown learned to get around even this latitude. A jailer ordered to produce his prisoner can move him from one prison to another before the hearing, or better: send him to Jersey, Guernsey, Scotland, or overseas, outside the jurisdiction where the writ runs. An English subject can thus languish indefinitely without ever seeing a judge, as long as he remains out of reach of the court meant to protect him.

## A Fine Instead of a Promise

The law passed on May 27, 1679, under Charles II, bears a title that says it all: “An Act for the better secureing the Liberty of the Subject and for Prevention of Imprisonments beyond the Seas.” It turns the principle into mechanics. A jailer served with a writ of habeas corpus must produce his prisoner within three days, except for geographic exceptions, and state the grounds for the detention in writing. If he drags his feet or refuses, he forfeits one hundred pounds to the prisoner for a first offense, and two hundred pounds and his office for the second. And the transfer loophole closes at a stroke: sending an English subject prisoner to Scotland, Ireland, Jersey, Guernsey, or “any Parts Garrisons Islands or Places beyond the Seas” now exposes the sender to life imprisonment, disqualification from public office, loss of the right to a royal pardon, and five hundred pounds in damages to the victim.

## What the 1679 Act Shifts

What Magna Carta stated as a right, the 1679 Act turns into a quantified obligation, backed by penalties that the Crown itself cannot erase. It is this version, with its deadline and its fine, that crosses the Atlantic: in 1789 the United States Constitution directly takes up the English vocabulary by guaranteeing that “The Privilege of the Writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it.” A guarantee that protects only by stating the precise conditions of its own suspension: the lesson of 1679 is that a right that does not say who enforces it, and at what cost to anyone who ignores it, is not really a right.

repere.texte: First breach by a jailer: one hundred pounds to the prisoner. Second breach: two hundred pounds and the loss of his office.
repere.source: Habeas Corpus Act 1679 (31 Cha. 2 c. 2), Parliament of England

carte.punch: Sending a prisoner out of the kingdom put him beyond the reach of the law that protected him.
carte.idee: In 1679, England passes a law requiring every jailer to produce a prisoner within three days or pay a fine, and forbidding him to be sent out of the kingdom to escape that obligation. A right left abstract since Magna Carta becomes a quantified procedure.

quiz.question: Why does the 1679 Act specifically target the sending of prisoners “beyond the seas”?
choix: Because the Royal Navy was short of space in the kingdom's prisons
Because prisoners sent overseas got a faster trial
Because outside the kingdom, the writ of habeas corpus did not run and the prisoner escaped all judicial oversight
Because King Charles II wanted to develop the colonies with convict labor
quiz.explication: By sending a prisoner outside the jurisdiction where the writ ran, a jailer could exempt himself from any obligation to bring him before a judge; the navy, trial speed, and colonial settlement are not the reason given by the Act itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under which king and on what date is the 1679 Act passed?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Act is passed on May 27, 1679, during the reign of Charles II; its full title promises to better secure the liberty of the subject and to prevent imprisonments beyond the seas.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a jailer risk if he fails to produce his prisoner within the deadline set by the 1679 Act?
choix: A ten-pound fine, the same regardless of the number of breaches
One hundred pounds to the prisoner for the first breach, two hundred pounds and his office for the second
Immediate dismissal without a fine, from the first breach
A simple written reprimand, with no financial consequence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Act provides for a one-hundred-pound fine paid to the prisoner for a jailer's first breach, then two hundred pounds and the loss of his office for a second, a quantified penalty that replaces the simple reprimand.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What penalty does someone face who sends an English prisoner to Scotland, Jersey, or beyond the seas to remove him from the writ of habeas corpus?
choix: A one-hundred-pound fine, the same penalty as for a jailer who misses the three-day deadline
Six months in prison and a ban on staying in the town where the prisoner lived
Life imprisonment, disqualification from public office, and five hundred pounds in damages
Payment of the prisoner's transfer costs, with no other penalty under the Act
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For this specific case, the Act provides heavy, cumulative penalties: life imprisonment, disqualification from public office, loss of the right to a royal pardon, and five hundred pounds in damages to the victim.
